One pass over Nicosia

A real 1080p drone video went in. This came out. 1,199 frames decoded, 20 keyframes selected, 260,000 points reconstructed on a free GPU — and the far-field thinning you can see is the problem the brief actually poses.

Measured, not asserted

The far field thins out — by 6.6×

Switch the viewer to colour by range and the structure is obvious: dense near the camera, sparse toward the horizon. Point density per unit volume, measured across the whole 1.7 M-point cloud:

Range band (model units)PointsRelative density 

This is the requirement, not a defect An oblique single pass puts most pixels in the far field, where a monocular model has little parallax to work with. The problem statement names it directly — Key Challenge (i), “Limited viewing angles due to single flight path” — and exists precisely because “there is often only a single opportunity to capture data over the target area”. A planned survey grid is what you do not get.

What that implies for the deliverable

  • Report accuracy per range band, with per-point confidence. A 1 m claim that holds near the camera and fails at the horizon is not a single number.
  • The reconstructable swath is bounded by parallax, not field of view. An oblique frame sees to the horizon; it can only reconstruct a fraction of that. That boundary is the honest denominator for completeness.
  • Monocular metric depth becomes load-bearing. Where baseline is too weak to triangulate, a metric-depth model has to carry the far field — promoting it from optional densification to structural.

The slate gate had to be added after the first attempt: a title card passes a sharpness test, because black-on-white text gives a strong Laplacian response, so blur scoring alone let five seconds of credits straight into the keyframes.

And the blur gate did nothing here — 365 mean sharpness for selected frames against 361 for naive uniform sampling. This footage is gimbal-stabilised with no bad frames to reject. That gate earns its place on shakier input; on this clip it is inert.

The gap that remains

No GPS, so no georeferencing

Missing input This clip carries no GPS track, so the model above is metric-relative only — there is no absolute frame to place it in and no ground truth to score against. That is a missing mandatory input, not the wrong kind of footage. The problem statement lists GPS as mandatory precisely because without it the task is unsolvable as stated.

What closes it: a single-pass video with per-frame GPS, ideally RTK, plus a LiDAR or multi-pass reference to score against. The pass being oblique and unplanned is correct — that is the brief.
